## Archiving and registering a reanalysis {#every-reanalysis-leaves-a-public-trail}

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
**OSF**, the Open Science Framework: a public repository in which data, code and **registrations** are timestamped and citable.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
A registration is a **frozen, dated snapshot of a plan**. Anyone can check what you said you would do, and when.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
You need no account today. We read OSF the way that reviewers do.
:::
::::

::: notes
Outside a classroom, an analysis plan is preregistered by filing it in a public registry, and the Open Science Framework is the registry that most social scientists meet first. The OSF does two jobs. It archives materials, and the SCORE programme and its robustness study keep their records there, which is why you can stand in the place of one of its analysts at all. It also registers plans, and a registration is a frozen, timestamped snapshot of what you intend to do, filed before you do it, which nobody, you included, can edit afterwards. [advance] You need no account for any of this today, since we read the OSF as a reviewer or a sceptical reader would, starting from the public record of our paper.
:::

## The preregistration of the robustness study {#the-study-you-are-inside-was-preregistered}

::: {.small}
- The robustness study: **100 claims × at least 5 independent analysts**, no instructions on how to analyse
- The scoring rules – same conclusion? effect size close? – were **registered on the OSF after the analysts had been recruited and before any analysis began**
- Outcome: 74% same conclusion; 34% within ±0.05 *d*
:::

::: {.src}
Preregistrations osf.io/4ev9t (pp. 2 and 9) and osf.io/y4evp; @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness [p. 136].
:::

::: notes
The robustness study, in which you have been working as the sixth analyst, was itself preregistered, with a hundred claims, at least five analysts for each, and complete freedom of analysis in the first task. What had to be fixed in advance was the judging, what counts as the same conclusion and how close an effect size has to be. Those rules were registered on the OSF after the analysts had been recruited and before any of them had started, among them the rule that two results count as the same when their effect sizes lie within five hundredths of a Cohen's d of each other. Because nobody could change the criteria once the results were in, the seventy-four per cent and the thirty-four per cent that we met earlier can be taken at face value.
:::

## Preregistration templates {#two-templates-one-choice}

::: {.small}
- In your report: the **AsPredicted short form**, adapted for data you already hold – eight plain-language questions (on OSF: "Preregistration Template from AsPredicted.org")
- The fuller tool for a reanalysis: the **secondary-data template** (van den Akker et al. 2021, *Meta-Psychology*) – 25 questions, built for analysing data you already hold
- Both templates are in your reading
:::

::: notes
The workshop uses one of two templates. The preregistration block in your report follows the AsPredicted short form, eight questions in plain language, but AsPredicted was written for people who have not yet collected their data, and its first question, whether any data have been collected, has for us the awkward answer that we already hold everything. The secondary-data template by van den Akker and colleagues, with twenty-five questions and a whole section on what the analyst already knows about the data, was built for that situation, and a full version of this exercise would use it. Our block borrows that section and calls it the data-in-hand statement.
:::
